description.sr_latin: Kuhinjski razgovori, srpska jela, i kako da pohvališ nečiju kuhinju.
description.en: Kitchen conversations, Serbian dishes, and how to compliment someone's cooking.

phrases.context: You and your partner are both home and hungry — suggest you just cook a meal together.
phrases.notes: 'Hajde da' + present = 'let's' in casual Serbian. Bosnians say 'kuhati' / 'kuhamo' where Serbians say 'kuvati' / 'kuvamo'.

phrases.context: You're both standing in the kitchen at dinnertime — ask your partner what the two of you will cook.
phrases.notes: 'Pravimo' = we make/are making; present tense covers both English forms. 'Praviti' is the everyday verb for making food.

variations.en: What are we going to make?

phrases.context: You're splitting up the prep work at the counter — tell your partner who does what.
phrases.notes: 'Sečem' = I cut (present), 'mešaj' = stir (command). Serbian uses plain present for near-future like 'I'll chop'.

phrases.context: You've just tasted something your partner cooked and it's great — give a warm general compliment.
phrases.notes: 'Odlično' is the neuter form agreeing with 'ovo' (this thing). A safe, all-purpose compliment.

phrases.context: First bite of a meal your partner cooked — blurt out your instant verdict on the taste.
phrases.notes: 'Ukusno' = tasty (neuter), used on its own as 'delicious'. Add 'mnogo' — 'mnogo je ukusno' — to pile it on.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend just plated something impressive — tell her cooking really comes naturally to her.
phrases.notes: Literally 'cooking goes well to you' — '<thing> ti dobro ide' is the Serbian frame for 'you're good at <thing>', with 'ti' in the dative.

phrases.en: Can I have a bit more?
phrases.context: Your plate's empty and the food was great — angle for seconds, which doubles as a compliment.
phrases.notes: 'Može' literally = 'it can', but it's the all-purpose 'okay / can I' word. Here it floats 'can I get a bit more?'

phrases.sr_latin: Hajde da bacimo ćevape na roštilj.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Хајде да бацимо ћевапе на роштиљ.
phrases.en: Let's throw some ćevapi on the grill.
phrases.context: It's a warm afternoon and you're craving grilled meat — propose firing up the grill for ćevapi.
phrases.notes: 'Ćevapi' (sing. 'ćevap') are small grilled minced-meat fingers, served in lepinja with onion and kajmak. The word and dish are Turkish, from 'kebab'.

phrases.sr_latin: Niko ne pravi sarmu kao tvoja baka.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Нико не прави сарму као твоја бака.
phrases.en: Nobody makes sarma like your grandma.
phrases.context: You're eating the family's cabbage rolls and they're perfect — praise whose recipe it is.
phrases.notes: 'Sarmu' is accusative of 'sarma', cabbage rolls of minced meat and rice. 'Sarma' is Turkish, from 'sarmak' (to wrap).

phrases.en: Do you want a pljeskavica or ćevapi?
phrases.context: You're both at the grill counter deciding what to order — ask your partner which classic they'd rather have.
phrases.notes: Both objects sit in the accusative after 'hoćeš'. 'Pljeskavica' is a big spiced meat patty — the Balkan burger.

phrases.context: There's a jar of red pepper spread on the table — ask whether it was made at home, which would be a real compliment.
phrases.notes: 'Domaći' = homemade, the gold standard; families cook ajvar in huge autumn batches. 'Ajvar' is a Turkish-origin word for the roasted-pepper relish.

phrases.sr_latin: Burek je samo sa mesom. Ostalo su pite.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Бурек је само са месом. Остало су пите.
phrases.en: Burek is only with meat. The rest are pies.
phrases.context: Someone calls a cheese pastry 'burek' at the table — set them straight on what the word covers in Serbia.
phrases.notes: 'Sa mesom' is instrumental (the 'with' case). In Serbia a cheese version is 'pita sa sirom', never 'burek' — a hill many will die on.

phrases.en: Shall we go get burek for breakfast?
phrases.context: It's morning after a late night out — suggest grabbing fresh pastry from the bakery instead of cooking.
phrases.notes: 'Burek' is a Turkish loanword (börek). In Bosnia it's beloved too, but there 'burek' can mean any filled pastry — the opposite of the Serbian meat-only rule.

phrases.sr_latin: Treba nam još luka i paprike.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Треба нам још лука и паприке.
phrases.en: We need more onions and peppers.
phrases.context: You're checking the kitchen before a shop and notice the basics are running low — say what's missing.
phrases.notes: 'Treba nam' = 'we need' (literally 'is needed to us', dative 'nam'). 'Još' forces the genitive on 'luka' and 'paprike' — the 'more of' case.

phrases.sr_latin: Možeš li da skočiš do prodavnice?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Можеш ли да скочиш до продавнице?
phrases.en: Can you pop by the store?
phrases.context: You need one quick thing and your partner is closer to the door — ask them to nip out to the shop.
phrases.notes: 'Skočiš' literally = 'you jump', used colloquially for 'quickly nip over'. 'Do' takes the genitive, so 'prodavnice'.

phrases.en: We have nothing in the fridge.
phrases.context: You open the fridge, find it bare, and announce it to your partner so you can plan a shop.
phrases.notes: 'U frižideru' is locative ('in the fridge', no motion). Double negative 'nemamo ništa' is standard and correct in Serbian.

phrases.sr_latin: Probaj ovo, jel' treba još soli?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Пробај ово, јел' треба још соли?
phrases.en: Taste this, does it need more salt?
phrases.context: You're mid-recipe and unsure about the seasoning — hand your partner a spoon and ask their verdict.
phrases.notes: 'Probaj' = taste/try (command). 'Još soli' is genitive after 'još' — 'more salt', the 'some more of' case.

phrases.context: You're handing over a pan straight off the stove — warn your partner before they grab it.
phrases.notes: 'Pazi' = watch out (command). 'Vruće' is the neuter 'hot', agreeing with an unstated 'it' (the pan or food).

phrases.en: Turn the heat down a bit.
phrases.context: The pot is bubbling over and about to boil too hard — tell your partner to dial the stove back.
phrases.notes: 'Smanji' = reduce/lower (command). 'Vatru' literally = 'fire' (accusative) — the everyday word for stove heat.

phrases.context: You poke at the dish and reckon it's cooked through — tell your partner your verdict.
phrases.notes: 'Mislim da' = 'I think that'. 'Gotovo' is neuter 'done/finished', the usual call for food that's ready.

phrases.context: You walk in starving and head for the kitchen — ask your partner what food is around.
phrases.notes: Impersonal 'ima' = 'there is'. 'Za jelo' = 'to eat', literally 'for food'; 'jelo' is the everyday word for food or a dish.

phrases.context: Dinner's almost ready and you're starving — tell your partner just how hungry you are.
phrases.notes: 'Gladan' = hungry (masculine); say 'gladna' if you're female. 'Ko' is the casual short form of 'kao' (like/as).

phrases.context: Neither of you feels like cooking tonight — suggest just getting takeout instead.
phrases.notes: 'Naručimo' = let's order (perfective, one completed action), the natural choice after 'hajde da'.

phrases.context: Everyone's seated and about to start eating — say the word that opens the meal.
phrases.notes: Said before eating, to everyone. 'Dobar tek!' means exactly the same thing and is just as common.

phrases.context: The bread basket is down at the far end of the table — ask whoever's near it to hand it over.
phrases.notes: 'Mi' is the dative ('to me'), 'hleb' the accusative object. Serbians say 'hleb'; your Bosnian friend says 'hljeb'.

phrases.context: You've eaten plenty and the host is eyeing your plate for refills — politely signal you've had enough.
phrases.notes: 'Najeo sam se' is past tense and agrees with the speaker — 'najela sam se' if you're female. Expect 'Jedi još malo!' anyway.

phrases.context: A friend has just settled onto your couch — offer them a coffee the way every visit starts.
phrases.notes: 'Kafu' is accusative of 'kafa'. The word is Turkish; it usually means domaća, Turkish-style coffee, not espresso. Croatians say 'kava', Bosnians 'kahva'.

phrases.context: You're swamped in the kitchen and want a cup — ask your partner to put the pot on for you.
phrases.notes: 'Skuvaj' = literally 'boil', because Turkish-style coffee is boiled in a džezva, not brewed. Bosnians would say 'skuhaj'.

phrases.context: There's a lull in the afternoon and you want to catch up — suggest sitting down over coffee.
phrases.notes: 'Popijemo' is perfective 'drink up' (one finished coffee). Inviting someone 'na kafu' is as much about the chat as the caffeine.

phrases.context: You catch a whiff of smoke from the stove and realize the food's been left too long — call it out.
phrases.notes: 'Zagorelo je' is past tense, neuter to agree with an unstated 'it' (the food). 'Za-' marks the completed result.

phrases.en: I put in too much salt.
phrases.context: One taste tells you you've wrecked the seasoning — own up to your partner about what went wrong.
phrases.notes: 'Stavio sam' is past, agreeing with the speaker — 'stavila sam' if you're female. 'Previše' forces genitive 'soli'.

variations.en: I put in too much salt.

phrases.context: The dinner you were cooking is beyond saving — wave it off and propose the easy backup plan.
phrases.notes: 'Ma pusti' = 'forget it / never mind', a classic brush-off. 'Naručićemo' is future ('we'll order'), with 'picu' in the accusative.
